prompt: Put the four questions for reading an industry in the order the lesson asks them.
items: What decisions does this industry make over and over?
Where does the data come from, and what is odd about it?
trap: Starting from the industry's standard indicators is tempting, and it learns the vocabulary before knowing which decision any of it serves.

prompt: Why does the trap come last among the four questions?

choices.text: It is the least important of the four
choices.why: It is the one newcomers fall into; its place follows from what it is made of.

choices.text: It follows from the other three: an indicator, on odd data, used for a decision
choices.why: Right: once the first three are answered, the typical trap can be seen coming.

choices.text: Traps are found only after a dashboard has been built and used for a year
choices.why: The method aims to see the trap before the dashboard, not after.

choices.text: Regulators require it to be reported last
choices.why: No regulator is involved; the order is a reasoning order.

prompt: Which of these are what the lesson calls odd about a lender's data? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A loan's outcome arrives months after the decision
choices.why: Right: the decision is today, the answer is next year.

choices.text: Declined applicants are never seen again
choices.why: Right: the data describes the customers Ipê chose.

choices.text: Interest rates are recorded with too many decimals
choices.why: Not a habit that misleads anyone; decimals are not the issue.

choices.text: Fraud is confirmed weeks after the payment
choices.why: Right: labels arrive when the real card holder disputes the charge.

choices.text: Card payments are recorded once a month
choices.why: Payments are recorded as they happen; what arrives late is knowing which were fraud.

prompt: An analyst moves from Varanda to Ipê and starts by rebuilding Varanda's monthly sales review with loans instead of sales. What does the method say they skipped?
hint: Which question would have warned her?

choices.text: The indicators: loans have no target, so a review against target is meaningless
choices.why: Lenders set targets like anyone; the review shape is not the problem.

choices.text: The decisions: a lender takes no decisions every month
choices.why: It takes thousands a day; that is question 1's answer.

choices.text: The data: outcomes arrive late, so this month's loans look better than they are
choices.why: Right: a sale is complete when it happens; a loan is not, and a monthly total hides that.

choices.text: Nothing: a review of totals works the same in any industry
choices.why: The point of the method is that it does not; the data's habits differ.

prompt: Match each ratio with what it divides.
hint: Two of them divide by the book.

pairs.right: Interest earned minus funding cost, over the book

prompt: A lender with an average book of R$ 1,000 million lost R$ 30 million to bad loans in the year. What is its cost of risk, in per cent?
Ipê's efficiency ratio went from 33.9% to 31.4%. What does that say?

choices.text: Ipê became less efficient, since the ratio fell
choices.why: The efficiency ratio is cost over income, so lower means better.

choices.text: Its loans became safer
choices.why: Safety is the cost of risk, which got worse.

choices.text: It spends fewer reais of running costs per hundred reais of income
choices.why: Right: and it was true while profit barely grew.

choices.text: Its profit grew by about 2.5 points over the year
choices.why: Profit grew 3.8%; the ratio says nothing directly about profit.

prompt: Ipê's book grew 28.1% and income 21.2%, but profit before tax only 3.8%. Where does the lesson send the analyst to find out why?
hint: Which link of the chain grew fastest, and what explains it?

choices.text: To the loans grouped by when they were made
choices.why: Right: credit losses rose 64.4%, and only vintages tell age from quality.

choices.text: To the operating costs, which rose faster than income and ate into the margin of every product
choices.why: Operating costs grew slower than income; the efficiency ratio improved.

choices.text: To the fee income, which shrank
choices.why: Fees rose from 30 to 36.

choices.text: To the funding cost, which doubled when interest rates in the economy moved up
choices.why: Funding cost rose from 77 to 98, in line with the book.

prompt: Why can a personal loan made last month not be in default under Ipê's definition?
hint: 90 days overdue, and when the first instalment falls due.

choices.text: New customers are checked more carefully
choices.why: Maybe, but the reason here is arithmetic about time, not care.

choices.text: Its first instalment cannot yet be 90 days overdue
choices.why: Right: due after a month, 90 days overdue three months after that.

choices.text: Ipê leaves the first month out of its reports to avoid noise from late payments that are corrected quickly
choices.why: Nothing is left out; the loan simply has not had time.

choices.text: The law forbids calling a loan in default in its first year
choices.why: No such law in the lesson; the 90-day definition explains it.

prompt: A group of loans made in the same period, followed as it ages, is called a ___.
The headline 90+ rate is 2.31%, under the board's appetite of 4%. Why does the lesson say it means little on its own?

choices.text: Because 90 days is too long a definition
choices.why: The definition is fine; the lesson keeps it.

choices.text: Because the appetite of 4% was set for another product
choices.why: The appetite is for this book; the problem is what the rate is made of.

choices.text: Because a weighted average always understates the worst vintage in a book of loans
choices.why: Any average sits below its worst member; the specific problem is the young loans counted at zero.

choices.text: R$ 185 million of the R$ 394 million are too young to have defaulted
choices.why: Right: almost half the denominator cannot be in the numerator yet.

prompt: Ipê lent R$ 20, 24, 28, 32, 45, 60, 80 and 105 million in its eight quarters. What share of the total, in per cent, was lent in the last two quarters? One decimal.
hint: 80 + 105 over the sum of all eight.

prompt: At six months on book, the 2024 vintages averaged 2.2% and the 2025 ones 3.2%. What is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Nothing yet: the 2025 loans are younger, so they cannot be compared
choices.why: They are compared at the same age, six months; that is what vintages are for.

choices.text: Loans made in 2025 are going bad faster than 2024's at the same age
choices.why: Right: about half as fast again, the earliest warning a lender has.

choices.text: The headline rate will fall as the 2025 loans age
choices.why: As loans age they reach default; the headline will rise, not fall.

choices.text: The 2025 vintages are larger, which raises their rate by itself
choices.why: A rate is a share; lending more does not raise it on its own.

prompt: Comparing loans at the same months on ___ removes the advantage young loans have of not having had time to default.
hint: The x axis of the vintage curves.

prompt: A fraud rule flags 180 of a month's frauds and 2,820 good payments. What is its precision, in per cent? One decimal.
Rule A catches three frauds in four and yet 96 of every 100 alerts are good customers. Why?

choices.text: Good payments outnumber fraud a thousand to one, so 2% of them is far more than 300
choices.why: Right: the base rate. 2% of 399,600 is 7,992.

choices.text: The rule is badly written
choices.why: Any rule hunting something this rare looks like this; rule B does too.

choices.text: Fraudsters copy good customers' habits
choices.why: Perhaps, but the numbers follow from the base rate alone.

choices.text: The card processor reports fraud late
choices.why: Late labels affect counting, not why most alerts are wrong.

prompt: Rule A costs R$ 229,880 a month and the stricter rule B R$ 235,940. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: How close are they, and what is left out?

choices.text: Rule B, because its precision of 5.7% is higher
choices.why: Precision alone does not choose; the two mistakes have different prices.

choices.text: No rule, since both cost money
choices.why: With no rule the 400 frauds cost R$ 440,000.

choices.text: They are close, so the choice rests on the price of each mistake, set by its owners
choices.why: Right: a few reais more per blocked customer would flip it; the threshold is a business decision.

choices.text: Rule A, because the difference of R$ 6,060 a month settles it for good
choices.why: The difference is small next to a cost left out on purpose: customers who leave after being blocked.

prompt: A report on yesterday's card fraud shows a very low rate. Why does the lesson distrust it?
hint: When is a fraud known to be a fraud?

choices.text: Yesterday was a holiday
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson; the issue holds on any day.

choices.text: Fraud is confirmed when disputed, often weeks later
choices.why: Right: the labels have not arrived, the same young-book problem in another form.

choices.text: Daily rates are too small a sample to report at all, whatever the industry or the volume of payments
choices.why: Sample size can matter, but the lesson's reason is that the labels are late.

choices.text: Fraud rules switch off at night
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.

prompt: A customer earns a margin of R$ 500 a year, and 80% of customers stay each year. What is the simple, undiscounted CLV, in reais?
Comparison sites bring customers with a CLV of R$ 850 for an acquisition cost of R$ 650. What does that say?
hint: CLV/CAC, and that the CLV is undiscounted.

choices.text: A good channel: it returns R$ 200 per customer for certain
choices.why: Undiscounted and before any surprise in losses, R$ 200 is an upper bound, not a certainty.

choices.text: It barely pays back, and its customers leave fastest
choices.why: Right: a ratio of 1.3, with the lowest retention of the four.

choices.text: It is the best channel, because comparison-site customers are the most numerous ones in the report
choices.why: The table says nothing about numbers of customers; value per real is the question.

choices.text: Its CLV is wrong, since it is lower than its margin
choices.why: R$ 850 is 2.5 years of R$ 340 margin; nothing is wrong with it.

prompt: Referrals return ten reais of CLV per real spent. Why is moving the whole budget to referrals not the obvious answer?
hint: Average cost and the cost of the next one.

choices.text: Referral customers earn the lowest margin of the four channels
choices.why: Partner stores have the lowest margin, R$ 260.

choices.text: A ratio of 10 is a sign of a mistake in the data
choices.why: Nothing suggests an error; cheap acquisition is what referrals are.

choices.text: The next thousand referrals will not cost R$ 120 each, since friends to refer run out
choices.why: Right: R$ 120 is an average over referrals already made, as with lesson 15's paid search.

choices.text: CLV must be discounted first
choices.why: Discounting would lower every channel; it would not stop referrals leading.

prompt: A fast-growing buy-now-pay-later company reports a default rate falling every quarter. Using lesson 17's fourth question, what do you ask first?

choices.text: Whether its efficiency ratio is improving too
choices.why: A different indicator; it does not test the default rate.

choices.text: Whether its interest rates are higher than Ipê's
choices.why: Pricing does not explain why a default rate falls.

choices.text: Whether its customers are younger than Ipê's
choices.why: It is the loans' age that matters, not the customers'.

choices.text: How its vintages compare at the same months on book
choices.why: Right: a falling headline in a growing book may be youth, and only vintages tell.

prompt: Match each Ipê question with the indicator that answers it.

pairs.left: Are the newest loans worse than the old ones?
pairs.right: Default rate by vintage, at the same age

pairs.left: How much does the lending itself earn per real?
How many alerts of a fraud rule are right?
Which channel's customers are worth what they cost?
